query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered suitable for thin-film use, and its expense favors applying it as a protective coating on conventional metals rather than using it in bulk. Earlier studies examined room-temperature wear behavior in relation to coating–substrate combinations, composition, and grain size, but largely addressed the alloy itself or a limited thermal regime rather than the overall wear response of a coating across different temperatures. Under the constraints that FeNiCrCoCu remains a thin protective coating and that high-temperature wear is the target application, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its overall wear resistance and why? Specify an intervention relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the observations expected if the hypothesis is correct, state the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled pre-oxidation treatment that forms a uniform, nanocrystalline oxide layer on the FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coating will significantly enhance its high-temperature wear resistance by creating a load-bearing, self-lubricating barrier compared to the untreated coating.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited FeNiCrCoCu thin film on a conventional metal substrate with no pre-formed oxide layer.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled pre-oxidation thermal treatment (e.g., at 300–500°C under a defined oxygen partial pressure and dwell time) to form a nanocrystalline surface oxide layer.
generation.conditions: High-temperature wear tests conducted at temperatures above 200°C up to 500°C under standardized high-load conditions relevant to protective coating applications.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a uniform, nanocrystalline oxide (possibly spinel phase) layer on the surface.
generation.mechanism: The oxide layer acts as a self-adaptive protective barrier that bears load and reduces friction by providing a lubricious interface, thereby reducing wear rates under high-temperature conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Coatings that undergo pre-oxidation will exhibit significantly lower friction coefficients, reduced wear depth, and enhanced overall wear resistance compared to untreated coatings.
generation.baseline: As-deposited FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coating with no pre-oxidation treatment.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected to be observable only under high-temperature (200°C–500°C) and high-loading conditions; at lower temperatures, the benefits of the pre-formed oxide may be negligible.
generation.uncertainty: The exact oxide phase composition, optimal pre-oxidation parameters (temperature, oxygen partial pressure, and dwell time), and the magnitude of improvement remain to be quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set receives the pre-oxidation treatment to form the nanocrystalline oxide layer while the control set remains in the as-deposited state. Perform high-temperature wear tests (200°C–500°C) under identical high-load conditions using a tribometer. Characterize the friction coefficient and wear depth via real-time monitoring and post-test surface profilometry, and verify the oxide layer via microscopy.
measurements: Friction coefficient over time during wear tests
Wear track depth and volume via profilometry
Microstructural analysis of the oxide layer via SEM/TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized samples do not display a statistically significant reduction in friction and wear or if the oxide layer formation does not correlate with improved wear resistance compared to the baseline coating, then the hypothesis is falsified.

decision.trend: Early work on high-entropy alloy coatings largely focused on room‐temperature wear and emphasized variables such as substrate interactions, composition tweaks, and grain size control. More recent studies (e.g., PMC7515071 and PMC7304825) expanded the exploration to high-temperature wear, revealing that at elevated temperatures, oxide formation (or phase transformations) can dramatically alter the wear response. The trend shows a move from purely mechanical descriptors at ambient conditions toward incorporating temperature‐induced surface chemical or microstructural modifications as key contributors to wear resistance.
decision.unsolved: While high-temperature wear behavior has been probed through overall friction and wear depth measurements, there remains an incomplete understanding of the mechanism: specifically, whether and how a self-forming, fine-scale oxide layer acts as a dynamic, load-bearing, and self-lubricating surface that governs the overall wear resistance of thin-film FeNiCrCoCu coatings. The missing link is a testable, mechanistic link between controlled oxide formation (or its suppression) and the measured improvements in wear performance under high-temperature, high-load conditions.
decision.lever: Introduce a controlled pre-oxidation thermal treatment on the as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coating to form a uniform, nanocrystalline oxide surface layer (versus a baseline untreated coating) and perform high-temperature wear tests (e.g., >200°C up to 500°C under standardized high loading conditions). Key parameters to vary include the pre-oxidation temperature, oxygen partial pressure, and dwell time.
decision.why: This intervention directly tests the hypothesis that an in situ formed oxide layer—similar to the spinel phases observed in prior high-temperature wear studies—serves as a self-adaptive protective and lubricious barrier at service temperatures while remaining effective as a thin film coating. The controlled experiment will pinpoint the role of pre-formed oxide films in reducing friction and wear, aligning with prior evidence that high-temperature oxidation can enhance wear resistance, and would be falsified if the pre-oxidized coatings do not exhibit improved wear behavior compared to the baseline condition.
